summary: Describes how DHCP and BOOTP clients and servers interact, since DHCP does everything BOOTP does and more.

plainLanguage.summary: DHCP and BOOTP use related message formats, so their clients and servers can sometimes meet. This memo says how they should respond and what address rules protect BOOTP clients.

questions: can a dhcp server answer bootp clients
can a dhcp server serve bootp clients
how does dhcp work with bootp
subtitle: Rules for DHCP clients and servers that communicate with BOOTP participants.

tldr.problem: DHCP message formats are based on BOOTP, so DHCP and BOOTP clients and servers need rules for exchanging messages.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines how DHCP servers identify BOOTP requests and how either kind of client may use a reply from the other kind of server.
tldr.outcome: Server support for BOOTP clients is optional; automatic addresses for them must be configurable and default off, with an infinite lease if assigned.

today: RFC 1534 is a Draft Standard. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why DHCP and BOOTP Can Interoperate
sections.content: DHCP provides configuration parameters to hosts, and its message format is based on BOOTP. This means DHCP and BOOTP participants may exchange messages in some circumstances. The RFC defines the required behavior and refers to both BOOTP vendor extensions and DHCP options simply as options.
sections.plainLanguage: DHCP uses a message format based on BOOTP. That shared format lets the two systems exchange some messages, but they need clear rules for doing so.

sections.title: DHCP Servers Serving BOOTP Clients
sections.content:
A DHCP server treats a received message that includes the DHCP message type option as coming from a DHCP client. Without that option, it assumes the message came from a BOOTP client. A server may support BOOTP clients; if it is not configured to do so, it silently discards their BOOTREQUEST messages.

A supporting server may provide static addresses or automatic addresses selected from its pool. Automatic-address support must be configurable and default off. If it assigns an automatic address to a BOOTP client, it must give an infinite lease because that client does not know the DHCP lease mechanism. The server must send a BOOTREPLY, not a DHCPOFFER, and follow BOOTP rules.
sections.plainLanguage: A DHCP server can be set up to answer BOOTP clients, but it does not have to. If it gives one an automatically selected address, that address cannot expire through the DHCP lease mechanism.

sections.title: DHCP Clients Using BOOTP Servers
sections.content:
A DHCP client may use a reply from a BOOTP server if the returned configuration is acceptable. It must treat an IP address from that BOOTP server as having an infinite lease. When replies are available from both kinds of server, the client should prefer the DHCP server's reply.

The memo says that it does not discuss security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: A DHCP client may accept a suitable BOOTP reply. It treats the returned address as having no lease end and should prefer a DHCP server's reply when available.
